reference.title: Dear Graham
reference.text: Tracey is 24 and her partner is 46. They have a wonderful relationship, but he has already been married, had children and owned a business, and she is just starting her life. She wants to have children, but he isn’t sure. Should she leave him? Graham Norton answers her in his advice column (8.1).

reference.title: What’s the problem?
reference.text: Three people phone a radio programme and an expert gives them advice: Annabel and Peter, whose 25-year-old son still lives at home (8.5–8.6), Nick, whose girlfriend wants to move to London (8.7–8.8), and Jane, whose friend has invited somebody Jane doesn’t know on their holiday (8.9–8.10).

tasks.instruction: If you have a problem that you need to talk about, do you talk to a friend or to a member of your family? Why?
tasks.note: SB 1a — вопрос для обсуждения → разговор с ИИ

exercises.situation: You are a classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). You talk about who you go to with a problem. Ask the student: If you have a problem that you need to talk about, do you talk to a friend or to a member of your family? Why? Who exactly? Do they give good advice? React with interest and ask one or two follow-up questions. Then give your own answer: you usually talk to your best friend Lucy, because she is a good listener and she doesn’t tell anybody, but for money problems you talk to your dad. Use short, simple sentences. If the student makes a mistake with should (e.g. She should to listen, She shoulds), repeat the correct form naturally in your reply.
exercises.goal: Say who you talk to when you have a problem and why.
exercises.opener: Hi! If you have a problem, who do you talk to – a friend or somebody in your family?
criteria: says who they talk to (a friend or a member of the family) and gives at least one reason with because
gives a little more detail (who exactly, what kind of problems, what advice they get)
reacts to the partner’s answer or asks a question back

steps.example: I usually talk to my sister.
Because she’s a good listener and she always gives good advice.

tasks.context:
Dear Graham, I’m 24 and my partner is 46. We’ve been together for two years, and we have a wonderful relationship. I also have a great relationship with his children from his previous marriage. But I feel worried when I think about our future together. He has already lived life. He’s been married, he’s had children, and he’s owned a business. I’m just starting my life. I want to have children, but he’s not sure. I love him and I want to be with him, but I also want to share the adventures of life with someone. Should I leave him? Am I making my life more difficult by choosing to be with someone who’s more than 20 years older than me? Tracey

What should Tracey do?
a She should leave him and find somebody who is nearer her age and shares her interests.
b She should think hard about what kind of man she really wants to be with before making a decision.
c She should stay with him if she loves him. Being with an older man has advantages as well as disadvantages.

exercises.prompt: Which advice do you agree with? Answer in 2–4 sentences and say why.

questions.text: Which of the three pieces of advice do you agree with?
questions.hint: (I agree with… I think she should…)

questions.text: What do you think she shouldn’t do?

criteria: says which advice (a, b, or c) they agree with and gives at least one reason
uses should / shouldn’t + infinitive without to correctly at least twice
uses I don’t think she should… (not I think she shouldn’t…) if they give negative advice

exercises.situation: Role play for an English class (level: pre-intermediate). The student is the expert on the radio programme ‘What’s the problem?’. You play three callers, one after another. 1) Annabel: your son Jamie is 25, a chef, still lives at home because renting a flat is too expensive, gives you only a little money for bills, and now wants to go on a two-week holiday to Mexico with his friends. Should you tell him he can’t go? 2) Nick: you’ve been with your girlfriend for three years; she wants to move from Bolton to London to get a better job and wants you to come, but you have a good job and a good salary in Bolton. Should you follow her or stay? 3) Jane: you planned a holiday in Turkey with your old friend Susan, but Susan has invited another friend, Angie, whom you don’t know, and she didn’t ask you. What should you do? Tell each problem in 3–4 short sentences, then ask What should I do? Listen to the advice, react (That’s a good idea / But I don’t want to…), and ask one follow-up question before you say thank you and move on to the next caller. If the student says should to or I think you shouldn’t, repeat the advice naturally with the correct form (you should go… / I don’t think you should…).
exercises.goal: Give advice to three callers with should.
exercises.opener: Hello, is that ‘What’s the problem?’? I’m Annabel. We’ve got a son, Jamie, and he’s 25…
criteria: gives each caller at least one piece of advice with should / shouldn’t + infinitive without to

reference.title: should / shouldn’t
rows: She’s very stressed. She shouldn’t work so hard.
You shouldn’t drink coffee in the evening. It’ll keep you awake.
I think you should get a new job.
I don’t think you should speak to him.

reference.text: Use should / shouldn’t + verb (infinitive without to) to give somebody advice or to say what we think is the right thing to do. should / shouldn’t is the same for all persons: I should, she should, they should.

reference.title: Negatives and questions
reference.text: Negative: should not → shouldn’t: You shouldn’t make a decision in a hurry. Question: put should before the subject: Should I leave him? What should I do? Don’t use do / does.

reference.title: I think / I don’t think
reference.text: We often use I think you should… or I don’t think you should… to give advice. For negative advice use I don’t think you should…, NOT I think you shouldn’t…

reference.title: ought to
reference.text: You can also use ought to / ought not to instead of should / shouldn’t, e.g. You ought to leave your boyfriend. She ought not to work so hard.

reference.wrong: I think you shouldn’t speak to him.
reference.right: I don’t think you should speak to him.
reference.why: With think, make think negative, not should.

reference.wrong: You should to see a doctor.

reference.title: get
reference.text: get is one of the most common verbs in English. It has several different meanings, e.g. arrive, become, and can also be used with many prepositions or adverbs with different meanings, e.g. get up, get on with.

reference.title: get
rows: get angry, get divorced, get fit, get lost, get married, get nervous, get ready
get better / get worse, get colder
get a job, get a newspaper, get a ticket
get into (out of) a car, get on (off) a bus, get on with (somebody), get up
get home, get to school, get to work
get an email (a text message), get a present, get a prize

tasks.instruction: Ask and answer the questions with get
tasks.note: SB 5c → разговор с ИИ: ИИ задаёт вопросы книги, в конце ученик спрашивает сам

exercises.situation: You are a classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). You ask the student some of these questions, one at a time, and react to the answers with interest (Really? Me too!), sometimes giving your own short answer: When was the last time you got a present? What was it? Who was it from? Do you usually get nervous before exams or presentations? What do you do to feel more relaxed? What website do you use if you want to get tickets to travel or for the cinema, theatre, or concerts? Who do you get on with best in your family? Is there anybody you don’t get on with? How do you get to work / school / university? How long does it usually take you? What’s the first thing you do when you get home? How many messages do you get a day on your phone? Who are they usually from? Do you have a good sense of direction, or do you often get lost? Ask 5–6 questions, then let the student ask you two questions with get. If the student says get to home, repeat the correct phrase naturally (get home).
exercises.goal: Answer questions with get, then ask two yourself.
exercises.opener: Hi! When was the last time you got a present? What was it?
criteria: answers at least five questions in full sentences with the correct get phrase (got a present, get nervous, get on with, get to work, get home, get lost…)
uses the right tense of get (got for the past, get / gets for routines)
asks the partner at least two questions with get

steps.text: Answer about presents, exams and tickets
steps.example: I got a book from my brother for my birthday. I always get nervous before exams.

steps.text: Answer about your family and getting to work
steps.example: I get on best with my sister. I get to work by bus – it takes about 20 minutes.

steps.text: Answer about getting home, messages and getting lost
steps.example: When I get home, I have a shower. I get about 50 messages a day. I often get lost!
How do you get to work? Do you often get lost?

exercises.prompt: What time did you **arrive at** the station?

exercises.explain: become + adjective = get + adjective.
